strengths: The paper addresses a natural and practically motivated gap: computing sliced Wasserstein distances from sample streams under memory constraints. The bridging of the quantile sketching literature (KKL sketches) with sliced optimal transport is a clean and sensible design, exploiting the quantile-function representation of 1DW.

The theoretical analysis is complete and self-contained: probabilistic bounds for streaming CDF/quantile estimation (Props. 1–2), streaming 1DW and transport map (Props. 3–4), Stream-SW (Cor. 1), and the MC variant (Thm. 1) are all proven in the appendix, and the space/time complexity analysis (logarithmic in stream length, linear in sketch size) is clearly stated.

Experiments cover a reasonable breadth: approximation error against closed-form SW (Gaussians, mixtures, MNIST), streaming point-cloud classification, streaming gradient flows with W2 scores, change-point detection on MSRC-12, and runtime scaling up to 2M atoms, where full SW becomes infeasible.
The paper is generally well organized, and limitations of the theory (compact support) are explicitly discussed and complemented by non-compact empirical experiments.
weaknesses: The novelty claim of being the 'first' streaming estimator for 1DW/Stream-SW needs careful substantiation. Quantile sketches have long been used for approximate distribution comparison on streams in the database/streaming literature, and W1 between one-dimensional projections is essentially an L1 quantile-function discrepancy; the paper should more thoroughly survey and differentiate from prior streaming Wasserstein/quantile-based distance estimators.

The theoretical guarantees rely on compact support with diameter R; for unbounded distributions no approximation bounds are given, only empirical evidence. Since the target applications (IoT streams, real data) do not come with a known diameter R, the practical relevance of the guarantees is limited. Moreover, constants are hidden, so the bounds do not give actionable sketch-size guidance beyond k = O((1/ε)√log(1/δ)).

The main experimental baseline is only SW with random subsampling at matched retained-sample budget. The motivating comparison — Compressed Online Sinkhorn — is discussed at length as impractical but never empirically compared, and other plausible streaming baselines (e.g., reservoir sampling, adaptive/optimized projections, online Sinkhorn with compression) are absent. This weakens the empirical case that the quantile-sketch machinery is the right tool rather than simply a better subsampling scheme.

Some empirical results raise questions: in Table 7, 'SW (random sampling)' is orders of magnitude slower than full SW despite retaining far fewer samples (e.g., 36.8s vs 0.37s at n=50k), suggesting the baseline implementation is not comparable, which undermines the runtime claims. Also, Stream-SW's pure-Python implementation is far slower than GPU full SW in feasible regimes, and the paper does not state whether code is released.

The contribution is somewhat incremental in technical depth: the theory is largely a composition of known KKL sketch guarantees with the quantile representation of 1DW, plus standard concentration arguments. The application experiments (500/300 point clouds, four gesture subjects) are small in scale.

Presentation has notable rough edges: typos ('we also can form', 'empricial'), the one-sided variant (Defs. 3–4, Appendix B) requires the full empirical quantile function of one side and thus does not fully satisfy the streaming motivation for that case, and Definition 3's notation is inconsistent (arguments k2 retained though unused).

strengths: The paper addresses a natural and underexplored question — estimating the sliced Wasserstein distance from data streams under memory constraints — and the bridging of quantile sketching (KKL sketches) with sliced OT is a sensible and, to my knowledge, novel combination.

The theoretical treatment is relatively complete for a conference paper: probabilistic bounds for streaming CDF and quantile estimation (Props. 1–2), streaming 1DW and transport maps (Props. 3–4), a population-level bound for Stream-SW (Cor. 1), and an MC-projection guarantee (Thm. 1), with full proofs in the appendix and a complexity analysis (space logarithmic in stream length).

The experiments cover four settings (Gaussian/MoG approximation error, point-cloud KNN, gradient flows, change-point detection) and consistently show Stream-SW dominating random subsampling at matched memory, with a runtime study (Table 7) demonstrating scalability to 2M atoms where full SW runs out of memory.
The idea is conceptually simple and the paper is largely self-contained; the one-sided variant and gradient-approximation discussion (Appendix B) add practical flexibility.
weaknesses: The key motivating baselines are never empirically compared: the introduction criticizes Online Sinkhorn (Mensch & Peyré, 2020) and Compressed Online Sinkhorn (Wang et al., 2023) at length, yet all experiments compare only against random subsampling. The claim that Stream-SW is the practical streaming solution is therefore not substantiated against the existing streaming OT literature.

Several proofs are loose or contain gaps. The bound in Prop. 2 (Eq. 11) depends on γ_{q,ε}, which can vanish (e.g., at atoms or median regions), making the pointwise quantile guarantee vacuous in exactly the regimes of interest; the transition from (11) to the integrated bound (12) relies on an identity between L1 of quantile functions and the CDF integral that is asserted ('proven in Appendix A.1') but not actually shown. Eq. (40) (a^p − b^p ≤ p·max{a,b}^{p−1}(a−b)) is applied where a−b may be negative, and the compact-support step (35) compresses a sup-based argument into a single line. These need careful repair or at least precise statements.

Proposition 1 as stated is inconsistent with its proof: the statement is a pointwise bound (∀x) while the proof establishes the stronger uniform sup bound (Eq. 27); the constants are also only loosely traced (e.g., Eq. 26 yields 6n²/k², not 24n²/k², from the preceding line).

The streaming setting is somewhat artificial in the downstream experiments: ModelNet10 point clouds and ShapeNet shapes are static datasets artificially fed as streams, and only one real streaming dataset (MSRC-12, four subjects, a single change point) is used for change-point detection. Generalization of the change-point conclusions from four individuals is weak.

All theory is for compactly supported distributions (diameter R), yet the headline applications (Gaussians, MNIST in 784d, 60d gesture data) are non-compact; the empirical section does not connect back to the theory, and the constants C_{p,R} are not characterized, so the practical value of the bounds (e.g., how to choose k for a target ε) remains unclear.

Presentation quality is below the bar: numerous typos ('empricial', 'Bernouli', 'can also can form', 'inequalty'), garbled equation typesetting in the supplement, and an unfinished placeholder section header ('C. Additional Experiments — Closed-form for Gaussians' with no content under it) suggesting a rushed submission.

Reproducibility is limited: no code release is mentioned, implementations are described only anecdotally (pure-Python compaction, PyTorch GPU SW), and the runtime comparisons conflate implementation quality with algorithmic complexity (the paper itself concedes 'substantial room for further speed improvements').

The claimed 'first streaming SW estimator' may overstate novelty given the substantial prior work on streaming quantile estimation (Greenwald–Khanna, KKL) on which the construction directly rests; the contribution is essentially an application of an existing sketch to an existing distance, with theory that mostly re-derives known sketch guarantees plus a triangle inequality to W_p.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: computing sliced Wasserstein distance from data streams is a natural gap, and the paper convincingly identifies why existing streaming OT approaches (Online Sinkhorn, Compressed Online Sinkhorn) are impractical in low-memory settings (O(n) memory, expensive measure compression).

The key technical insight is clean and elegant: because 1DW has a closed form via quantile functions, streaming quantile sketches (KKL sketches) can be composed with slicing to yield the first streaming SW estimator. This bridges two literatures in a way that feels principled rather than ad hoc.

Solid theoretical development: probabilistic guarantees are given at each level of the construction (CDF estimation, quantile function estimation, streaming 1DW, transport map, Stream-SW, and the Monte Carlo version), culminating in Theorem 1 with the expected error bound O(min{k1, k2, sqrt(n), sqrt(m), sqrt(L)}^{-1}) under compact support. Proofs are provided and mostly straightforward but correct applications of Hoeffding/DKW inequalities combined with union bounds.
Honest complexity accounting: the space complexity O(L(k + log(n/k)) + Ld) and near-linear time complexity are clearly stated, including the caveat that practical time depends on implementation.

Experiments cover approximation error (with closed-form ground truth for Gaussians, mixtures, and MNIST), streaming point-cloud K-NN classification, streaming gradient flows with W2 scores, and streaming change point detection. Stream-SW consistently outperforms the random subsampling baseline at matched retained-sample budgets, and the runtime analysis (Table 7) demonstrates scalability to 2M atoms where full SW runs out of memory.
Appendix materials are complete: full proofs, one-sided variant, gradient approximation recipe, additional experiments, and hardware description, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The main empirical baseline is SW with random subsampling of 3k + 2log(n/(2k/3)) samples. This is a weak comparison: other natural baselines such as reservoir sampling, adaptive/stratified subsampling, or quantile-based subsampling (which would likely also improve on uniform sampling) are not considered, and neither streaming competitor (Online Sinkhorn, Compressed Online Sinkhorn) is empirically benchmarked despite being the primary motivation in the introduction.

The theoretical guarantees require compactly supported distributions with diameter R, and all constants (C_{p,R}, c_{p,R}) are unspecified and likely degrade with R. The approximation-error experiment (Section 4.1) is on Gaussians without compact support, which is complementary but leaves a gap between the theory and the empirical setting; the dependence of the error on the support diameter is never probed empirically.

The bound in Theorem 1 is rate-optimal in k, n, m, L only in the sense of expectation under strong assumptions; the constant factors and the R-dependence may limit practical guidance on choosing k. The paper provides little discussion of how to select k in practice beyond the empirical sweeps.

Some experimental evidence is thin: the gradient flow uses only 3 runs and a single shape pair from ShapeNet; the change-point detection uses only 4 subjects with a single change at a known time index 500 and no false-alarm rates or variance reported in Table 3; the change-point baseline (sliding window) is not a strong streaming competitor. Statistical significance of the improvements is not assessed.

A methodological concern in the gradient flow experiment: the target distribution's sketch is treated as fixed during optimization, and the streaming estimator's bias is inherited by every iteration, yet the theory only bounds the estimation error, not the error accumulated along the flow. The paper does not analyze or discuss this compounding.

No public code release is mentioned, and the compaction is implemented in pure Python without optimization; this limits reproducibility and weakens the runtime claims, although the honest discussion of implementation immaturity is appreciated.

Several proofs lean on randomness assumptions about the KKL sketch (e.g., independence of the ξ_{i,h} in Equation (23) and the variance bound in the proof of Theorem 1) that are inherited from Karnin et al. (2016) but not carefully restated; the argument that W_{p'}^p difference is bounded via a^p − b^p ≤ p max{a,b}^{p−1}(a−b) is fine, but the overall error constants combine somewhat loosely (e.g., the jump from (55) to (56) obscures the R-dependence in b).

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: estimating sliced Wasserstein distances from single-pass sample streams with bounded memory. The proposed Stream-SW is, to my knowledge, the first streaming SW estimator, and the combination of KLL quantile sketches with the quantile-function representation of 1DW is natural and well-motivated.

The theoretical treatment is fairly complete: probabilistic guarantees are provided for streaming CDF estimation (Prop. 1), quantile function estimation (Prop. 2), streaming 1DW (Prop. 3), streaming transport maps (Prop. 4), streaming SW (Cor. 1), and the Monte Carlo projection approximation (Thm. 1). The proofs in Appendix A are careful (e.g., the uniform-over-x argument via grid + union bound, the mean-value-theorem handling of |a^p - b^p|), and complexity analysis is given for both space and time.

Experiments cover multiple settings: approximation error on Gaussians, Gaussian mixtures, and MNIST digits; streaming point-cloud KNN classification on ModelNet10; gradient flows on ShapeNet; and change-point detection on MSRC-12. Stream-SW consistently outperforms the random-subset baseline in approximation error, classification accuracy, and detection delay, and the runtime study (Table 7) demonstrates scaling to 2M samples where full SW fails with out-of-memory.

The runtime comparison honestly acknowledges that Stream-SW is slower than full SW when data fits in memory, and that the pure-Python implementation leaves speed gains on the table — a fair treatment of the practical trade-off.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is modest: the core contribution is plumbing the KLL sketch (Karnin et al., 2016) into the quantile representation of 1DW. Much of the theoretical work re-derives or restates KLL sketch guarantees combined with standard tools (Hoeffding, DKW, Monte Carlo rates); the constants in the bounds (e.g., C = 1/144) are loose, and the main guarantees require compact support, limiting direct applicability.

The empirical baseline is weak. The only comparator is SW with random subsampling sized to match the KLL sketch bound. No comparison is run against the streaming OT methods the paper motivates against (Online Sinkhorn, Compressed Online Sinkhorn), nor against alternative streaming summaries (reservoir sampling variants, Greenwald–Khanna sketch, coreset methods). This makes it hard to judge how much of the gain is specific to KLL sketches versus any principled streaming quantile method.

The theoretical guarantees assume i.i.d. samples and fixed distributions, yet two of the showcased applications (gradient flow, change-point detection) involve drifting/non-stationary streams, and the change-point experiments use the one-sided variant whose approximation guarantees are not established. This gap between assumptions and applications is not discussed in a limitations section, which is notably absent from the paper.

Experimental scale and rigor are limited: the change-point study uses a single dataset with four subjects and a single change type; the gradient flow uses two shapes and three runs; several comparisons (e.g., Table 3 delays) lack variance estimates or significance testing. No code release is mentioned, which weakens reproducibility given implementation-sensitive claims (e.g., the counterintuitive runtime decrease as k grows from 100 to 1000).

Presentation has recurring sloppiness: typos ('can also can form', 'depending onp and R', misused 'in turn'), notation overload for the many variants of W and SW with hats/oversets, and an Impact Statement and computational-infrastructure appendix that are essentially placeholders. Some claims in the abstract ('more accurate approximation of SW than random subsampling, with lower memory consumption') are stated as general facts but are only demonstrated on specific synthetic/dataset cases.

strengths: The paper addresses a natural and practically motivated problem — estimating the sliced Wasserstein distance from sample streams under memory constraints — and it appears to be the first attempt to do so, which gives the contribution clear novelty of problem setting.

The methodological bridge between streaming quantile approximation (KLL sketches) and the quantile-function representation of 1DW (Eq. 3, 5) is clean and well-motivated; the resulting algorithm is simple and the one-sided variant (Appendix B) is a useful addition.

The paper provides a fairly complete theoretical treatment: probabilistic bounds for streaming CDF estimation (Prop. 1), quantile estimation (Prop. 2), streaming 1DW (Prop. 3), the transport map (Prop. 4), and Stream-SW with MC projections (Theorem 1), with proofs included in the appendix that largely follow standard tools (Hoeffding, DKW, union bounds) applied carefully.

The experimental section covers several downstream tasks beyond distance approximation (streaming KNN classification, gradient flows, change point detection) and includes a runtime study (Table 7) showing that Stream-SW scales to millions of atoms where full SW runs out of memory, which supports the claimed scalability.
The comparison against random subsampling is roughly memory-matched (retaining 3k + 2 log(n/(2k/3)) samples), which makes the accuracy comparison in Figure 3 and Tables 4–6 reasonably fair.
weaknesses: The central technical building block (KLL sketch) is an established data structure with known guarantees; the contribution is essentially composing it with the quantile representation of 1DW, and the theoretical results follow from straightforward composition (Hoeffding/DKW plus union bounds). The theory is correct but not deep, and the constants (e.g., C = 1/144) make the bounds loose.

The guarantees have a structural limitation that undermines the streaming advantage: Corollary 1 gives an expected error of order min{k1, k2}^{-1} from the sketch quantization alone. Since the sampling error of SW itself is O(n^{-1/2}), to make the sketch error no worse than sampling error one needs k ≳ √n retained samples, which erodes the memory savings precisely in the large-n regime the method targets. The paper does not discuss this trade-off or when Stream-SW is genuinely preferable.

All theoretical guarantees require compact support of diameter R, with constants depending on R, yet the experiments are conducted on Gaussians and Gaussian mixtures (non-compact). The gap between assumptions and experiments is never addressed.

The empirical baselines are weak: the only comparator is SW with random subsampling (and full SW). No comparison with other memory-bounded strategies (e.g., merge-and-reduce, coreset construction, kernel thinning, quantization-based compression) is provided, and Compressed Online Sinkhorn (Wang et al., 2023), the closest prior streaming OT method, is dismissed in the introduction but never empirically compared. This weakens the claim that Stream-SW is the method of choice for streaming distribution comparison.

The experimental scale is modest: 500 training point clouds on ModelNet10 with KNN, a single pair of ShapeNet shapes for gradient flows with only 3 runs, and change point detection on 4 subjects of a single dataset. Several results (e.g., Table 1 with ±1.3 to ±3.05 standard deviations on 3 runs, and Table 3 with single numbers) lack statistical rigor.

The reported runtimes actually show Stream-SW is much slower than full SW when data fits in memory (10.6s vs 0.37s at n=50,000), and the claimed advantage rests on a hypothetical memory-constrained deployment (IoT) that is never instantiated in the experiments. The pure-Python implementation also makes the runtime conclusions preliminary.
No code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility of the exact experimental pipeline; the computational infrastructure appendix (a single line) does not compensate.

Presentation quality is uneven: repeated typos ('we can also can form'), a boilerplate impact statement, no explicit limitations section, and several references to very recent/2026 arXiv preprints that reviewers cannot verify. The claims of being 'the first' streaming SW estimator are asserted rather than substantiated against the literature.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem: the paper appears to be genuinely the first to define a streaming estimator of the sliced Wasserstein distance, filling a real gap given that existing streaming OT methods (Online Sinkhorn, Compressed Online Sinkhorn) have O(n) or worse memory requirements.

Sound core insight: connecting the quantile-function representation of 1DW (Eq. 5) to quantile sketches (KLL) is a natural but effective bridge between the streaming-algorithms and SOT literatures, and the resulting method is simple and memory-efficient (space logarithmic in stream length).

Reasonably complete theoretical treatment: probabilistic bounds are given for streaming CDF estimation (Prop. 1), quantile estimation (Prop. 2), streaming 1DW (Prop. 3), the transport map (Prop. 4), and SW with MC projection estimation (Theorem 1), with full proofs in the appendix; the sample-complexity terms (min{k1,k2,√n,√m,√L}) are consistent with known results.

Broad empirical evaluation: approximation error on Gaussians/GMMs and MNIST, streaming point-cloud KNN classification, streaming gradient flows, and streaming change-point detection, plus a runtime study showing scalability to 2M atoms where full SW runs out of memory.
Honest discussion of practical limitations, e.g., the pure-Python implementation leaving speed on the table, and theoretical complexity vs. practical runtime.
weaknesses: Moderate conceptual novelty: the method is essentially the composition of a known data structure (KLL sketch, Karnin et al. 2016) with the known quantile representation of 1DW; the theoretical novelty is incremental, since Proposition 1's bound largely re-derives known KLL guarantees and the extension to 1DW/SW follows from the standard L1 duality between CDFs and quantile functions.

Experimental baselines are weak: the primary comparison throughout is SW with random subsampling at the sketch-size memory budget; stronger and more natural baselines (e.g., reservoir sampling of the same size, Greenwald-Khanna sketches, or other coreset/compression approaches) are absent, making it hard to judge how much of the gain is attributable to the specific sketch.

All guarantees require compact support of diameter R; behavior for unbounded supports (the practically relevant streaming case, e.g., Gaussians) is only addressed empirically, and the hidden constants in A_R, C_R, c'_{p,R} may be large, so the practical relevance of the bounds is unclear.

The change-point detection experiment (Table 3, Fig. 5) compares Stream-SW against a sliding-window SW baseline with different thresholding/bootstrap procedures, so the comparison is not apples-to-apples and the reported 'substantially better' detection delays may partly reflect the methodology rather than the streaming estimator itself.

No code release or reproducibility package is mentioned; details such as the exact compaction implementation, preprocessing, and seeds are thin (Appendix D lists only the hardware), limiting reproducibility.

Presentation issues: the proliferation of notations for variants (SWgp, SWdg, one-sided versions in Appendix B) is heavy; the uniformity argument in the proof of Proposition 1 (grid-based union bound over z_j^- points) is somewhat informal; and several citations (e.g., Nguyen 2026, Truong & Nguyen 2026) are to arXiv/2026-dated preprints of the authors.
